title: Numbers counted on one hand
title_target: លេខ និង លុយ — lék neng luy
goal: Master Khmer numbers — and understand why "six" sounds like "five-one": Khmer counts in fives, a legacy of the fingers on one hand.

dialogs.title: កិច្ចសន្ទនា — At the coffee stall across the street
dialogs.intro: Ani buys her first breakfast on her own. Listen carefully to the numbers: every time the vendor says a number above five, you will hear the word ប្រាំ (five) come first.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Counting in fives — why "six" sounds like "five-one"
body: Khmer counts on **one hand**. One to five have their own words; six to nine are formed by putting ប្រាំ (five) in front. This is not a cute curiosity — it is what you will hear every time you buy something, and beginners who haven't noticed it hear ប្រាំបួន (9) and think they are hearing two numbers.
after: ⚠️ Look at **seven**. It is written ប្រាំពីរ ("five-two"), but read *pram-pil*, not *pram-pii*. It is the only number whose sound changes, and it is exactly the one beginners mishear most often.
After ten, the pattern is regular again: ដប់មួយ (11), ដប់ពីរ (12), ដប់ប្រាំមួយ (16 — "ten-five-one"). Long, but no surprises.

grammars.title: The tens: the part not based on five
body: If the five-system ran all the way up, twenty should be "two tens". It isn't. **The Khmer tens were borrowed from Thai and Sanskrit**, and each has its own word to learn separately.
after: The good news: from thirty on, the pattern is regular again — សិប (*sep*) is "-ty", and you just change the number in front. ⚠️ Only ម្ភៃ (20) truly stands alone and contains no សិប at all. That one word you simply have to memorize.

grammars.title: ⚠️ ម៉ឺន and សែន — two units English doesn't have
body: English jumps from thousand straight to million. Khmer slips two units in between, and both are used every day for prices.
after: So when a vendor says ពីរម៉ឺនរៀល, your brain has to translate it as "two × ten thousand" = 20,000 riel, not "two thousand". ⚠️ Getting one of these units wrong at the market means paying ten times the price.
The good news: **ដប់ពាន់ (ten thousand) is also used** and fully understood, especially by younger people in Phnom Penh. If you're not sure of ម៉ឺន yet, use ពាន់ and you'll be safe.

sections.title: Money in Cambodia: two currencies in one wallet

blocks.text: Cambodia uses **riel and US dollars side by side**, and you will get change in a mix of both all day long. It's confusing in the first week, then it becomes routine.

head: Rule of thumb
Details
rows: The rate hardly ever changes; just count 4,000.
Coffee, noodles, short tuk-tuk rides, bottled water.
Change under 1 dollar is always in riel
US coins don't circulate in Cambodia at all.
⚠️ Check your bills — even a dollar with a small tear is often not accepted.

blocks.title: Two habits that save a lot of confusion
items: **Ask the vendor to write the number down.** សូមសរសេរលេខ (*soum saa-sé lék*). Khmer numerals ០–៩ are on the script pages of this course, and most vendors write with the familiar Western digits anyway.
**Always repeat the number aloud before paying.** The vendor will nod or correct you. This is a normal habit in Cambodia, not a sign that you don't trust them.
